draft_text:
The title alone contains three scripts: Chinese, Arabic, English. 胡(هو / who) are you? It reads like a translingual pun that collapses into a question about identity — the Chinese character 胡 historically denoting foreignness, the barbarian, the other; the Arabic هو meaning "he" or "him"; and the English "who" sitting between them as both homophone and genuine interrogative. [~This trilingual wordplay follows a pattern consistent with Slavs and Tatars' long-standing engagement with what they call "transliteration as politics"|based on extensive documentation across Frieze, e-flux, Art-Agenda, and monograph texts spanning 2009–2024~]. It is a title that asks you to read it aloud, to hear how different writing systems arrive at the same sound, and to wonder what gets lost — or found — in that convergence.

Slavs and Tatars, the collective behind this exhibition opening at Rossi & Rossi on 21 March 2026, have spent nearly two decades working in precisely this territory: the slippage between languages, the politics buried inside alphabets, the identities that emerge from the cracks between empires. Founded in 2006 as a reading group — not a studio, not a collective in the usual sense, but a group of people sitting together with books — they carved out a geographic and intellectual focus that remains singular in contemporary art. Their stated area of interest: the space between the former Berlin Wall and the Great Wall of China. A vast, largely post-Soviet, post-Ottoman, post-imperial swathe of the world that encompasses Central Asia, the Caucasus, Iran, and the Turkic and Slavic peripheries. This is not a region that Western art institutions typically know how to frame, which is partly why Slavs and Tatars have proved so useful to those institutions, and partly why the collective's best work exceeds the frame entirely.

Their practice has always resisted easy categorisation. They publish books — serious, designed, essayistic objects that function as artworks. They give lecture-performances that combine academic rigour with absurdist humour, a combination that owes something to both the Central European cabaret tradition and the Islamic rhetorical form of the maqama. Their installations tend to involve language made physical: neon signs in multiple scripts, inflatable sculptures that literalise linguistic metaphors, carpets woven with slogans. The conceptual engine driving all of it is a conviction that language is never neutral, that the choice of script — Cyrillic versus Latin versus Arabic — carries the weight of colonial and anti-colonial projects, of forced modernisation, of belonging and exclusion.

Berlin, where the collective is based, makes particular sense as both home and subject. This is a city whose own history of division maps imperfectly but suggestively onto the larger partitions that Slavs and Tatars explore. The Wall that split Berlin was also, in a sense, a linguistic border: the same German language pressed into service by two opposing ideological systems. And contemporary Berlin, with its large Turkish, Arabic-speaking, and post-Soviet populations, remains a place where scripts and tongues jostle daily — on shopfronts, on bureaucratic forms, in the code-switching of ordinary conversation.

Rossi & Rossi, the gallery hosting the exhibition, brings its own resonances. Founded in London in 1985 by Anna Maria Rossi and later joined by her son Fabio, the gallery built its reputation first through classical Indian and Himalayan art before expanding into contemporary Asian practices from 2005 onwards. [~The gallery's Berlin presence and specific programming history are less extensively documented than its London and Hong Kong operations|sourced primarily from the gallery's own site and a handful of art press mentions~]. The pairing with Slavs and Tatars makes a certain geographic and intellectual sense: a gallery whose expertise lies in the art of Asia's interiors meeting a collective whose entire project is about those interiors' entanglement with the West.

What to expect in the gallery space itself is, at this stage, partially speculative — Slavs and Tatars tend to reveal installations close to opening. But their recent trajectory offers clues. Over the past several years, the collective has deepened its engagement with what they term "affective politics" — the way bodily practices like prayer, laughter, digestion, and speech physically enact ideological positions. Their 2022–2024 cycle of works drew heavily on the politics of the mouth: language as something produced by the body, involving tongue, teeth, breath. Given the title's explicit play on phonetic resemblance across scripts, this exhibition likely continues that somatic thread. Expect sculptural work that makes language tangible, text that demands to be sounded out, and the collective's characteristic wit — a quality that distinguishes them from the more po-faced corners of politically engaged art. [~This projection is pattern-based, drawn from programming notes and reviews of their last five institutional shows|not confirmed by any preview material for this specific exhibition~].

The 胡 character is worth dwelling on. In classical Chinese, it designated the nomadic peoples to the north and west — a catch-all for the non-Chinese, the foreign, the uncivilised. It appears in words for pepper (胡椒, literally "barbarian spice"), for the fiddle (胡琴, "barbarian stringed instrument"), for nonsense (胡说, "barbarian talk"). It is a single character that contains centuries of othering, and yet it has also been reclaimed, worn with pride, absorbed into everyday vocabulary to the point where its original derogatory force has faded into etymology. To place this character next to its Arabic near-homophone and its English echo is to perform, in miniature, exactly the kind of operation Slavs and Tatars have always been interested in: showing how a sound travels across civilisations, picking up and shedding meaning as it goes.

There is a risk, of course, that this kind of work becomes a comfortable niche — the clever multilingual art collective that Western institutions can programme when they want to signal geopolitical literacy. Slavs and Tatars are aware of this trap; their writing and interviews frequently address it with a self-awareness that can itself become a kind of armour. The real test of any new exhibition is whether it pushes past the established formula, whether the linguistic play opens onto something genuinely unsettling rather than merely ingenious. Their best work does this: it leaves you uncertain about your own language, your own alphabet, the sounds you take for granted as natural rather than political.

Opening on the spring equinox — a date of transition, of equal dark and light — 胡(هو / who) are you? arrives at a moment when questions of identity, allegiance, and belonging feel simultaneously urgent and exhausted. We have had a decade of identity discourse. We have had the backlash to the discourse. What Slavs and Tatars offer is something older and stranger than either: a reminder that identity has always been a matter of which script you write your name in, which direction your letters travel across the page, and which empire decided that your language needed reforming. The question in the title is not rhetorical. It is genuinely asking. And the answer, as the three scripts suggest, depends entirely on who is listening.
critique_assessment: Strong essay with genuine insight and a confident voice, but needs factual corrections on the gallery's history, trimming of some decorative passages, and better source transparency — publishable after rework.

critique_issues.fix: The source material contains ZERO usable information about the Rossi & Rossi gallery. The 'venue context' is about Aldo Rossi the architect and IBA 1987 in Friedrichstadt — completely unrelated. The claim that the gallery was 'Founded in London in 1985 by Anna Maria Rossi and later joined by her son Fabio' and 'built its reputation first through classical Indian and Himalayan art before expanding into contemporary Asian practices from 2005 onwards' is not supported by any provided source. This smells like a hallucination — suspiciously specific founding date, family narrative, and pivot year. The confidence marker on this paragraph acknowledges limited sourcing but still presents fabricated-sounding details as fact. Strip all unverifiable biographical claims about the gallery. Keep only what can be reasonably inferred: Rossi & Rossi is a Berlin gallery hosting the show.

The 'artist background' source material contains information about Hugh O'Connor (a marine painter from Michigan) and Barry O'Neil (a medical illustrator from the Bronx) — neither of whom has any connection to Slavs and Tatars. The essay wisely ignores this garbage data, but the editor should note: any claims about Slavs and Tatars' specific exhibition history (the '2022–2024 cycle of works' focused on 'politics of the mouth') are not verifiable from the provided sources. The essay's confidence marker partially covers this, but the specificity of the '2022–2024 cycle' claim needs flagging or softening.

The claim that the Berlin Wall was 'in a sense, a linguistic border' is a stretch. East and West Germany shared a language with minor bureaucratic/ideological vocabulary differences, but calling the Wall a 'linguistic border' overstates the case. The essay hedges with 'imperfectly but suggestively,' which helps, but the paragraph still leans on a metaphor that doesn't quite hold. Tighten the framing — the Wall was an ideological partition, not a linguistic one, and the analogy works better if stated more carefully.

This paragraph is mostly guesswork dressed up in confident language. 'Expect sculptural work that makes language tangible' is generic enough to describe any Slavs and Tatars show from the past decade. The confidence marker is honest, but the paragraph still reads like padding. Either commit to a more specific argument about where their practice is heading (and why this show's title signals a particular direction), or cut the paragraph significantly and fold the useful bits into the 胡 analysis.

'Opening on the spring equinox — a date of transition, of equal dark and light' is tourist-brochure mysticism. The equinox detail is fine as a fact but the poetic gloss adds nothing and feels like filler. Cut 'a date of transition, of equal dark and light' entirely.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 9 — 'We have had a decade of identity discourse. We have had the backlash to the discourse.'
critique_issues.fix: This is good — punchy, specific, argumentative. But the follow-up ('What Slavs and Tatars offer is something older and stranger than either') drifts into vague praise. What exactly is older and stranger? The essay gestures at script politics but doesn't land the final punch hard enough. Sharpen the ending so the 'older and stranger' claim is concrete.

critique_issues.location: Paragraphs 2-3 — background on Slavs and Tatars
critique_issues.fix: Two full paragraphs of background before the essay gets to anything new. The reading-group origin story and the 'Berlin Wall to Great Wall' line are well-known to anyone who has encountered this collective. Compress these into one paragraph and get to the 胡 analysis faster — that's where the essay's real thinking lives.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 8 — 'a self-awareness that can itself become a kind of armour'
critique_issues.fix: This is a strong observation but the sentence structure around it is flabby. 'Their writing and interviews frequently address it with a self-awareness that can itself become a kind of armour' — 'frequently address it with' is weak. Tighten.

This is the essay's best paragraph and its real argument. The etymology of 胡椒, 胡琴, 胡说 is specific, illuminating, and does real intellectual work. But it deserves even more space — the connection between the semantic drift of 胡 (from slur to everyday prefix) and the broader project of Slavs and Tatars could be drawn tighter. This is where the essay earns its existence.

Several sentences exist only to transition: 'Their practice has always resisted easy categorisation' (paragraph 3 opener) is a cliché. 'Berlin, where the collective is based, makes particular sense as both home and subject' (paragraph 4 opener) is throat-clearing. Cut or rewrite these.
